Things are very much not back to “normal.” In the 1990s, the federal debt-to-GDP ratio was roughly half of what it is today. Even then it raised enough fiscal alarm that a Republican Congress and President Clinton worked toward zero deficits—and briefly achieved a surplus.

Today the picture is far more severe. The U.S. faces a simple, inescapable arithmetic problem. Federal tax receipts have historically hovered around 17–18% of GDP regardless of statutory rate changes. Non-discretionary (mandatory) spending already stands at roughly 14% of GDP. At a debt-to-GDP ratio near 100% and with 10-year yields in the 4–5% range, debt service alone consumes about 3.3% of GDP today and is projected to rise toward 4.5% or higher.

Taken together, mandatory spending plus interest already absorb virtually all federal tax revenue, leaving almost nothing for discretionary spending. And much of what Congress labels “discretionary” is in practice non-negotiable. The result is a structural predisposition toward perpetual deficits.

This is the fundamental reason the United States will eventually have to scale back its global economic and military footprint and ask allies to carry more of the load. Doing so will erode the dollar’s exorbitant privilege and raise the long-term cost of borrowing.

This is not a normal cyclical problem. It is a long-term recipe for fiscal crisis and, if left unaddressed, economic ruin. The country can still coast for a while on sheer size, economic dynamism, and inertia. But we should not kid ourselves: we are on an extremely abnormal and unsustainable path. 

So much so that even the historically fiscally responsible voices seem to thrown in the towel and accepted it as fait accompli and resorted to praying for a technological miracle like AI somehow miraculously saving us all. I think they’ll likely be disappointed. I like the techoptimists, I am one myself. Alas most of the tech people, albeit clearly smart in their own right, just have no idea how economics works even at a basic level bc they never studied it.

By now most people accept that stablecoins are simply better money. Instant settlement, cross border payments... that arguments been won. 

But the most important use case is that they're programmable.

We're heading into an agentic economy. Billions of AI agents doing real economic work, hiring each other, paying each other, thousands of times an hour at machine speed. An agent can't open a bank account. An agent can't handle dollar bills. You simply cannot have an agentic economy without programmable money.

@chadcascarilla puts it perfectly in this clip. Marc Andreessen said software would eat the world... if that's true, software eats money too. And software eating money looks like a stablecoin, not the system we've got.

This is the crux of my Exponential Age framework. An entirely new economy is being built for machines, and it needs its own money, its own rails, its own everything.
